project_description: A lightweight, un-opinionated React.js component library comprised of element and layout primitives. The components are designed to be context agnostic and flexible while still having simple APIs. This library is open source and under active development, however the current version is stable and available for download via the NPM registry.

images.alt_text: A laptop sitting ontop of a polished concrete floor with large brass service pipes in the background, displaying a UI mockup of a program created using the Mattkleyn component library.

videos.url: URL or path to project image

case_study.content: Background information

This component library was initially part of my Portfolio V2 React migration project – a complete re-design and architecture overhaul. One defining requirement was that the portfolio needed to have the capacity to easily change layouts, styling, and composition without major structural rework in the code.

With flexibility being the primary driver in the component designs, they quickly ballooned with props to account for various use cases, however this creates components that do a lot of things but nothing well. To maximise flexibility and minimise complexity meant that they would need to be context agnostic and have clear separation in responsibilities – thereby separating element primitives and layout primitives. By keeping to primitives, I was able to minimise prop drilling and kept the component API clean while also ensuring the primitives could be used across multiple use cases.

A further realisation was that any future projects would go through the same iterative component design and development process, essentially duplicating the code many times over across the various codebases. Additionally, with the ‘fragmented’ nature of the codebases, refactoring a components’ design to a newer, better alternative, would require a lot of refactoring, styling issues and potential crashes across each project.

Due to these initial requirements, I saw an opportunity to split the project cleanly into two codebases, a component library that I could reuse across multiple projects, and the portfolio which would be a consuming project with its own needs and requirements. By having a dedicated dependency, the same UI code would not need to be created every time which would be a massive time save.

This would also enable me to build a system that would speed up future projects, ensure consistency within consuming projects, and enable any component modifications to be easily propagated to each consuming project and therefore avoiding multiple refactors to integrate new component designs. A single system would also scale easily with the addition of components to tackle any emerging requirements and aid with maintenance and optimization.
The Mattkleyn Component Library was created out of opportunity rather than constraint.
Project objective and requirements

With the slew of existing component libraries like ShadCN, Radix or Chakra-UI, the question becomes, why not use an existing framework that already has a community, is supported by maintainers, is optimised for accessibility, and also responsive out of the box. Building my own component library has a few distinct advantages, I would have:

content: Full control over the API and prop requirements
An experimental area to gain a better understanding of React component library design and implementation across various use cases
A component library that is uniquely suited to how I produce code and structure projects, meaning there is no learning curve to implementing a new and foreign framework into a project
A library that would evolve with me, my requirements and my style as a developer

case_study.content: This meant that the design and availability of the components would need to be such that any project could use them without prop or class bloat, would need to be used in a variety of contexts without breaking or limiting the implementation, and still be powerful enough to warrant the effort in creating a bespoke library. Additionally, each API would need to be predictable, from a name and behaviour perspective - intuitive. Further the library would need some base styling out of the box but be easily overridden by the consuming app to not constrain any project into a specific style.

The main goal is to create a re-usable and highly flexible component library that will decrease the UI development time of a consuming app while maintaining consistency and quality. To achieve this goal, the following specifications were considered for the overall architecture and component design:
Architecture and system design
Tokens, classes, and variants

CSS tokens are heavily implemented to enforce styling consistency across components. By ensuring the components styles utilize variable which in turn point to tokens, the token can either be swapped for another token, or the token value can be modified to create site wide themes or to propagate specific value changes throughout the site.

Each component has a ‘className’ prop to inherit base styles, and variant styles which are differentiated through Block-Element-Modifier (BEM) naming conventions. This separation of responsibility makes it easy to override variant styles without affecting base styles and enables pseudo polymorphic behaviour. Further adding in utility classes or custom classes is also possible through this prop to allow total flexibility and control over each component styles.

To ensure predictable behaviour, the naming of the various classes and tokens were kept being as explicit as possible to avoid any confusion as to the effects. Variants specifically follow BEM naming conventions to differentiate the CSS styles for readability purposes.

Lastly, the specificity of the classes on each component is also kept as low as possible to allow easy overrides without having to resort to using ID selectors or ‘!important’. This is achieved with minimising nested CSS properties and combo classes and avoiding ID selectors for base styles. While having base styles applied, are maintained to be un-opinionated and context-agnostic to keep the library lightweight.
DX considerations

Composition is heavily favoured over configuration. By keeping the components to their primitive forms instead of complex components, prop drilling is almost entirely avoided, making the component behaviour predictable and easy to reason about. Further the components are split into element primitive and layout primitives. This separates the responsibilities and keeps the component APIs clean and predictable. This approach also further enforces the idea of composability, as complex components can be easily made by utilizing any combination of these primitives. Lastly, by minimizing prop bloat and allowing the user to add in custom props – more below – the component API stays clean and minimizes cognitive load which can lead to confusion and frustration during development or maintenance.
API design

As a general rule, the components kept as uncontrolled components to keep them ‘dumb’. This makes it necessary for the parent component to monitor the child’s state and act as a co-ordinator component. This avoids the necessity to lift state and keeps the primitive component behaviour predictable, while also avoiding prop explosion to account for x-many states and event listeners.

Each component is also allowed to accept custom props through the API by de-structuring addition props within the component. This feature allows for the potential to create more and bespoke props on a per use bases which can be highly contextual, directly limiting prop bloat and keeping the API clean.

The component element tags follow semantic rules, by using <button>, <section>, <figure> tags etc. This works with screen reader capabilities and allows for out of the box accessibility consideration.

To allow for further flexibility, components are polymorphic, using the ‘as’ prop, which is tied to the element tag effectively allowing the user to choose the correct semantic tag for that context, whether it is a <section>, <aside>, or <article> for example. This enables the same component to be rendered under a multitude of contexts, increasing use cases and avoided ‘niche’ or one time use components. This consistency in API implementation makes the library intuitive to use and limits the learning curve for effective use.

case_study.alt: Image of the as tag and its API usage.
case_study.caption: Fig 1: The 'as' prop enables polymorphic behaviour within the components, allowing the user to specify the correct semantic tag for the context.

case_study.content: Motion integration

Motion is very specific to the UI design, as such the component library is kept to only include micro-interactions on elements such as buttons, and links. To keep to similar paradigms, the motion design on the included components, also consume motion tokens. This helps to create a design system that is not only flexible but also extensible with the capacity to be highly bespoke. Motion tokens include duration scales, and easing curves. The included micro interactions on currently limited to hover, press, and focus states.

Component interactions, UI animation, page loads, and even scroll based animations are intentionally excluded from the library due to the variability of the animations in terms of degree, scale, and even number of actors. This would be better suited to a motion specific design system.

A challenge arose from a conflict in scroll engines. The component library – specifically ModalRoot component – utilises native scroll to lock the background while open. When attempting to implement Lenis in the consuming app, the native scroll was overridden by the Lenis virtual scroll. This is a currently an unresolved conflict, and as such the component library will most likely continue to be scroll engine agnostic and use native scroll. A patch would be required for users that require smooth scrolling from libraries such as Lenis.
Build system
The library is in the MVP phase and still under active development, however it is published on the NPM registry for use.

Initially the library utilized Vite for building and transpiling, however on every build run, Vite would hoist and install its own React dependencies which would conflict with the consuming app. Attempts were made to rollback vite versions to react agnostic versions, however that was unfruitful. It seemed that Vite was not fit for purpose for a component library being published to NPM. In response, Tsup was utilized as the bundler of choice as it externalized React without hoisting like in the case of Vite, and it still enabled fast building, simplicity and dts support which would be helpful when migrating the library to Typescript – more below. Additionally, Tsup automatically supports tree shaking, which helps to ensure that consuming apps only ship with components actually utilized, instead of the entire library. Lastly, the build output is structured to provide clean ES modules and type definitions, making the library easy to consume in modern React projects.
Results
While anecdotal, the implementation of this library in a consuming application has shown positive results:

content: The speed of developing context specific components is faster
The simplicity of the component primitives has thus far not been a limiting factor in terms of UI design or programming logic
The API design pattern consistency makes the components easy to use and intuitive
Component refactoring and maintenance is greatly improved as the library acts as the single source of truth
By keeping to element and layout primitives, element duplication is avoided and this composability allows for a great deal of flexibility in the consuming app
This library is now the UI foundation for future consuming projects.

case_study.content: Future improvements

The component library contains a standard set of components that are most commonly utilized. However, this library will constantly expand with new primitives and potentially new UI components such as sliders, accordions, dropdown menus to speed up more specific UI patterns.

Likewise common motion component patterns will also be added to the component library for the same reason. However, a design challenge will be keeping the motion components simple in their implementation but still flexible enough to allow for complex animations. Animation co-ordinators are also planned in the form of ‘global scroll managers’ or motion-based component maps for example.

Responsive behaviour is an important item that I need to resolve with the components, however coming up with a responsive design system that translates across projects may be challenging due to it being heavily dependent on the UI design across breakpoints. The current default behaviour is only through fluid responsive spacing and typography scales, which can be easily overridden via changing the variable value, just like in the case of the base styles.

The biggest overall change is a Javascript to Typescript conversion which is planned over the next couple of months. The use of Typescript will enhance development rather than the end result. Features such as autocomplete, d.ts file generation, explicit typing and compile time errors will also further assist the development experience.
From a usability perspective, JSDoc comments will feature in all components explaining component parameters, usage with examples - and when Typescript is integrated – expected return types.
Conclusion

As a proof of concept, the development and consumption of this React component library has been successful. The components have been easy to work with, override and composed into more complex components. The Typescript migration will also further help the development of the component library itself as explicit typing would influence the design of the components and even the API. Lastly, this component library now forms a solid basis to speed up frontend systems on future projects and will also give consuming apps the flexibility to make changes to those user interfaces with minimal disruption to the code base. Despite the sheer number of available component libraries and UI frameworks, building my own component library and experimenting with the design of the components and system has been and interesting engineering and design challenge.

project_description: A Python based ETL pipeline that extracts and persists job postings from online job posting sites. A multi-phased rollout that is currently in the MVP phase, featuring a CLI UI, data persistence, and a single web scraper pipeline.  Future additions include a Python Flask web UI with user profiles and authentication, multi site extraction, LLM assisted extraction, email digest, automated job application workflows, and potential upskilling recommendations.

images.alt_text: A laptop and tablet sitting on a rustic looking shelf surrounded by nik naks, displaying a UI mockup of the JoSe program.

videos.url: URL or path to project image

case_study.content: Project objective

JoSe is a Python based ETL system designed to streamline job discovery by extracting, normalizing, and persisting job postings from multiple sources. The platform reduces the operational overhead of manual job search by automating data collection, applying structured relevance filters, and preparing the foundation for semantic extraction and automated application workflows.
Separation of concerns wasn’t optional; it was the only way to keep the pipeline adaptable as new sites and workflows emerge.
Background information

Job boards expose inconsistent structures, incomplete metadata, and fragmented filtering capabilities. Critical attributes—skills, experience level, role requirements—are often embedded in unstructured body text rather than surfaced as queryable fields. This inconsistency forces applicants to manually inspect each posting, significantly increasing time to relevancy.

JoSe addresses this by centralizing extraction across multiple sites and enforcing a consistent schema. The MVP focuses on a single extraction pipeline and CLI interface, with a roadmap that includes semantic enrichment via LLMs, multi site ingestion, and a lightweight Flask UI for visualization and user driven workflows.
Architecture and system design
JoSe is structured as a modular ETL pipeline with strict separation of concerns:

case_study.alt: A flow chart showing the code flow of the JoSe ETL pipeline.
case_study.caption: Fig 1: Flow chart of the systems data.

case_study.content: Extraction layer

The pseudo crawlers parse the DOM to retrieve link URLs from the job board HTML to handle pagination and dynamic content. Using this URL, the BeautifulSoup scraper extracts the available job data fields.
Normalization layer
Transformers standardize inconsistent HTML structures into a unified schema. This layer handles formatting, type coercion, and structural cleanup.
Acceptance layer
Business logic filters postings based on user defined parameters such as skills, geography, and experience level. This ensures only relevant records progress to persistence.
Persistance layer
PostgreSQL stores normalized records. A relational model was chosen over NoSQL due to the need for structured queries, schema evolution, and reliable filtering across multiple dimensions.
Pure scraping breaks under inconsistent HTML; a hybrid scraper LLM model delivers the reliability the domain demands.
LLM-augmented extraction (post-MVP)
Due to inconsistent HTML and missing metadata, JoSe will adopt a hybrid approach:

content: An LLM extracts structured fields according to a predefined schema.
Validation layers detect hallucinations, missing fields, and format deviations.

case_study.content: This hybrid model balances deterministic scraping with semantic understanding while controlling token usage and ensuring data quality.
Technology choices

Python was selected for its mature ecosystem in data extraction, transformation, ML integration, and lightweight web frameworks. PostgreSQL provides strong relational guarantees and scales cleanly with JoSe’s schema complexity.
UX/UI considerations
The MVP uses a CLI for rapid iteration, but the long term UX centers on a Flask based dashboard. The UI will prioritize:
The goal is to reduce cognitive load and surface actionable insights quickly.
Results
Early testing validated the architectural assumptions:

content: Pure scraping is insufficient due to inconsistent HTML and missing metadata.
Certain transformers (e.g., dates, locations) require semantic interpretation.
A hybrid scraper + LLM pipeline significantly improves extraction reliability.

case_study.content: The MVP established a stable foundation for multi site ingestion, schema enforcement, and future automation layers.

case_study.alt: A UML diagram indicating the module dependencies, and the integration of the LLM API
case_study.caption: Fig 2: Flow chart indicating the system module dependencies and LLM API integration.

case_study.content: Conclusion

JoSe demonstrates a scalable approach to automating job discovery through modular ETL design, structured data modelling, and planned semantic enrichment. While still in active development, the architecture supports future expansion into automated application workflows, recommendation engines, and richer data visualization. The system’s layered design ensures adaptability as new data sources, ML capabilities, and user requirements emerge.

project_description: A series of experiments in a collaborative setting to replicate existing websites using Webflow - a no/low code web builder tool. The premise was to replicate existing sites to focus on technical implementation across various philosophies, namely a standard approach, Finsweets Clients-First Framework, and Lumos. The replicas include the site layouts, responsive layouts, motion design, and CMS integration where applicable.

images.alt_text: Two desktop monitors sitting next to each other, each displaying a different replica from the project.

videos.url: URL or path to project image

case_study.content: Collaborators
Project objective

This project evaluated three Webflow development methodologies—Standard, Clients First, and Lumos—to understand their tradeoffs in scalability, maintainability, and developer experience. By replicating multiple real world sites across several months, we created a controlled environment to compare how each approach performs under consistent design, layout, and motion requirements.
Background information

The replicas were built collaboratively in a phased workflow: layout, responsive behaviour, and motion design. Each team member implemented the same site independently, allowing us to isolate framework behaviour from individual developer style. This repetition provided a reliable basis for comparing the philosophies behind each methodology rather than the execution of a single build.
Each methodology delivers value only when matched to the project’s scale, complexity, and post‑handover needs.
Project challenges and requirements

The primary challenge was conceptual: each framework required a shift in mental models, naming conventions, and structural assumptions. To reduce bias toward familiar approaches, we implemented multiple builds per framework. Additional constraints included coordinating across time zones and maintaining consistent evaluation criteria for layout fidelity, responsiveness, and maintainability.
Architecture and system design
Standard approach
A flexible, system agnostic method relying heavily on custom classes. It offers maximum freedom but requires strong discipline to avoid structural drift and long term maintenance issues.
Clients-First

Designed for non technical maintainers, it uses a standardized section structure with utility classes for adjustments. While predictable, the boilerplate introduces unnecessary nesting and fragmentation, increasing cognitive load without delivering proportional clarity.
Lumos
Lumos offers system level consistency at scale, but only when supported by disciplined component engineering and a mature design system.

A component driven philosophy optimized for large, complex sites. It enforces consistency through reusable components and variants but requires significant upfront planning, a mature design system, and experienced developers to avoid over engineering or variant sprawl.
Maintenance considerations

Clients First and Lumos both improve maintainability through standardized utilities and predictable patterns. However, Lumos trades initial flexibility for long term rigidity: once components are established, maintainers must work within those constraints. The Standard approach offers the opposite profile—high initial flexibility with higher long term maintenance risk if not tightly managed.
Developer experience (DX)

The Standard approach has the lowest barrier to entry but relies heavily on developer discipline. Clients First is accessible but requires understanding its structural boilerplate. Lumos demands the highest expertise due to its component engineering requirements, dependency on a robust design system, and the need to anticipate cross page behaviours and variant interactions.
Conclusion

Each methodology aligns with different project scales and team profiles. The Standard approach suits small projects with disciplined developers. Clients First benefits small to medium sites where non technical maintainers need predictable structures. Lumos excels in large, complex builds requiring consistency and system level thinking. No single approach is universally superior—the optimal choice depends on project complexity, team experience, and post handover maintenance requirements.

project_description: The Dev Frog Blog is a multi-user blog platform supporting full CRUD functionalites. All posts are persisted to a PostgreSQL DB, and are fully categorized with joined views tables. Further features include user profiles and authentication, OAuth, and server-side sessions.

images.alt_text: A laptop sitting atop a large rock deep in the forest, displaying a UI mockup of the dev frog blog platform.

videos.url: URL or path to project image

case_study.content: Project objective

Dev Frog Blog was designed as a scalable, full stack content platform built to support multi user publishing, dynamic routing, secure authentication, and persistent data storage. The system serves as a modular foundation for future expansion, including semantic search, user based recommendations, and machine learning driven content personalization.
The primary objective was to architect a platform that balances clarity, extensibility, and maintainability while supporting iterative feature development.
The system was designed as a modular platform that could evolve, not a one off CRUD assignment.
Background information

The project originated as a simple content site but quickly evolved into a multi phase system focused on architectural experimentation. Rather than treating it as a static CRUD assignment, the platform became a controlled environment for exploring system design patterns, data modelling, and scalable backend structures

Over successive phases, the system expanded to include dynamic server side rendering, REST inspired routing, PostgreSQL persistence, user authentication, Google OAuth integration, and secure session management. Each phase introduced new architectural considerations and informed the evolution of the codebase.
Project challenges and requirements
The platform needed to support:

Key challenges included designing a modular architecture from an initially monolithic codebase, implementing secure authentication flows, preventing destructive operations through recoverability mechanisms, and ensuring the system could scale as new features were introduced.
Architecture and system design

The system began as a monolith and was refactored into a modular architecture with clear separation of concerns. This restructuring enabled isolated testing, improved maintainability, and simplified the transition from JSON persistence to a relational PostgreSQL database.

case_study.alt: Flow chart indicating the flow through the REST routes and their respective endpoints.
case_study.caption: Fig: Flow chart indicating the flow through the REST routes and their respective endpoints.

case_study.content: Data modelling

The database schema was designed around atomic, purpose specific tables joined through SQL views. This approach reduced query complexity and improved performance by avoiding unnecessary joins in application logic.
Security

Authentication supports both traditional credential based login and Google OAuth. Passwords are salted and hashed using bcrypt, and all user input is validated and normalized before being passed into parameterized SQL queries to prevent injection attacks.
Sessions
Server side sessions (Passport) maintain user state securely while enforcing time based expiration to mitigate risk.
UX/UI considerations

The interface prioritizes clarity and low friction. Content creation flows are intentionally simple, with clear affordances for category selection, cancellation, and undoing destructive actions. Search functionality supports partial and case insensitive matching to reduce user frustration.
The visual layout draws from traditional editorial design, using a newspaper style structure to support long form reading while maintaining a modern, responsive experience.
Every UX decision was measured against a single question: does this reduce friction or create it?
Results
The final system delivers:

content: A fully functional multi user blog platform
Dynamic routing and server side rendering
Modular architecture prepared for future expansion

case_study.content: The platform now serves as a stable foundation for upcoming features, including semantic search, nested comments, and ML based recommendations.
Lessons learned and future recommendations

Early modularization significantly reduces refactor overhead and improves long term maintainability. Clear separation between layers—routing, business logic, data access, and rendering—proved essential as the system grew.

Future iterations will explore JWT based authentication, semantic search, and automated testing pipelines. Additional improvements include accessibility audits, expanded error handling flows, and further schema refinement.
Conclusion

Dev Frog Blog evolved from a simple content site into a scalable, modular platform designed for long term experimentation and architectural growth. While not intended as a production grade system, it successfully integrates modern backend patterns, secure authentication, and extensible data modelling, forming a strong foundation for future development and advanced feature integration.
